The word gutted is an adjective with two distinct meanings — one literal and one emotional. Both are important, and understanding them together will actually help you remember them better, because they are deeply connected.
Meaning 1: Literal — Having the insides removed or destroyed

When something is described as gutted, it means its interior has been completely removed, hollowed out, or destroyed — leaving only the outer shell.

Think of a fish at a market. Before cooking, a fishmonger removes all the internal organs. That fish is now gutted — empty inside, with only the outer body remaining.

The same idea applies to buildings and structures:

"The building was completely gutted by the fire."

This means the fire destroyed everything on the inside — the floors, walls, furniture, wiring — but the outer structure (the "shell") may still be standing. The building has been hollowed out.

More examples:

  • A gutted car → a car stripped of its engine, seats, and internal parts, leaving just the frame.
  • A gutted house → a house whose entire interior has been torn out, perhaps for major renovation.

The key idea: Something gutted is hollow. Its contents have been violently or completely removed.
Meaning 2: Emotional — Deeply devastated or bitterly disappointed

This is the more widely used meaning in everyday speech, especially in British and Australian English.

When a person feels gutted, they feel an intense, crushing sense of disappointment, loss, or devastation. It is not mild disappointment — it is the kind that hits you in the stomach and makes you feel hollow inside.

"I was absolutely gutted when I didn't get the job."

"She was gutted to hear that her flight had been cancelled."

"We were gutted when our team lost the final in the last minute."
Why these two meanings are connected

This is the beautiful part. The emotional meaning grew directly out of the literal meaning.

When you literally gut something — a fish, a building — you rip out everything from the inside and leave it empty. When a person feels emotionally gutted, it feels exactly like that — as if something has reached inside them and torn out their insides. They feel hollow, devastated, and empty.

So the emotional meaning is essentially a metaphor: "I feel as though my insides have been ripped out."

Very strong. Gutted sits at the extreme end of the scale of disappointment:

Mildly unhappy → Disappointed → Very disappointed → Gutted (devastated)

It is not a word you would use for small things. You would not say "I was gutted that the coffee was cold." You would say it for things that genuinely hurt — missing out on a big opportunity, losing someone important, hearing deeply bad news, failing at something you worked hard for.

The emotional sense of gutted is primarily British and Australian. If you use it with an American audience, they will likely understand it from context, but it is not a native part of American informal speech the way it is in Britain or Australia.

The literal sense (gutted fish, gutted building) is understood and used universally in English.
